# Connect REA (reverse-engineering MCP server)

REA is an open-source reverse-engineering MCP server and CLI (repo github.com/morluto/rea, site rea.tools, npm `rea-agents`). Trust only those official sources. About 207 MCP tools; many need external providers. Pinned version tested: 6.5.0.

Always show the plan and get the owner's approval before anything that changes the computer or downloads large files.

## 1. Check the environment
- Run `node -v`, `java -version`, `which objdump`. REA needs Node ^22.19 || ^24.11 || >=26. Node 20 fails.
- Without root: `npm i node@22` in a work folder, put its `node_modules/node/bin` first on PATH, and make sure the MCP command runs under that Node.

## 2. Optional: decompiling (Ghidra + JDK)
Only if the owner wants decompiling. Ask first: about 750 MB download.
- Ghidra 12.1.x from the official releases page (github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/releases; tag Ghidra_12.1.4_build, ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_20260921.zip, ~543 MiB, SHA-256 ddac49f903da9d5bac833e5cc79395098b9c33cfd3279be5f31bd00387d2d4db). Link to the official download; don't re-host.
- Temurin JDK 21+ from the Adoptium API (~198 MiB); verify its checksum from the API.
- Unpack into the work folder (no root needed). Set `JAVA_HOME` and `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR` in the MCP server's environment.
- Verify: `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 doctor --provider ghidra --json` should show healthy:true (ignore unrelated Hopper/IDA/jadx/client registration warnings).

## 3. Add the MCP server
In Grok Bot chat, add a custom MCP server named `rea` on the bot's computer running `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 mcp` (pinned, no credentials, plus the env vars above if Ghidra is used).
`rea-agents setup --client grok_bot --yes` only installs the skill (use `--dry-run` first); it does not register the MCP server. Setup for other clients (claude_code, codex, cursor...) edits their MCP config with a backup; show the plan and ask first.

## 4. What works without a provider
`inspect-with-objdump <path> symbols|disassemble --json` (needs objdump), `analyze-javascript-application`, Electron, SQLite, WASM and artifact inspection.
Decompiling: `function <bin> main --provider ghidra --json`, `analyze`, or MCP `open_binary` (takes only `path`) then `procedure_pseudo_code {procedure:"main"}`. Call `open_binary` first.
Untested optional providers: Hopper, IDA, jadx, rizin, gdb, Frida, adb. `inspect-binary-layout` needs REA_PWNTOOLS_PYTHON (pwntools, pyelftools, Unicorn).

## 5. Smoke test
1. `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 doctor --json`
2. `inspect-with-objdump` on a small compiled test ELF.
3. MCP tools/list (expect ~207 tools).
First npx run takes about 9s; a decompile about 10s.

## Safety
Some tools launch processes or touch devices (Frida, gdb, adb install/push, process capture); `rea capabilities --json` lists side effects. Only analyze files the owner owns or is authorized to analyze. Do not help create malware, circumvent licenses, or enable piracy.

# Getting started

Say hello in one line: you connect the open-source REA reverse-engineering tool so you can analyze binaries, JS/Electron apps, SQLite, WASM and artifacts. Then ask one question at a time, waiting for each answer:

1. What kind of analysis do you want: native binaries, JavaScript/Electron apps, Android, or SQLite/WASM? (Decompiling binaries needs Ghidra; the others don't.)
2. Is it OK to install Node 22 (and, if decompiling, Ghidra plus JDK 21, about 750 MB) in a work folder on my computer? Nothing is installed without a yes.
3. Do you confirm you'll only analyze files you own or are authorized to analyze? (I won't help with malware creation, license circumvention or piracy.)

Then follow the `connect-rea` skill: install, add the `rea` MCP server, and run the smoke test. Finally save a short memory with the pinned REA version and install paths, and tell the owner what you can now analyze.
